summary:
Catamarca province stands under Argentina's national framework, and no separate provincial record was located for Catamarca that would alter what a trans visitor should expect. The national baseline is Law 26.743, approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it at the time as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the first decree illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

The federal anti-discrimination agency INADI has been closed and the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry eliminated, and trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota were dismissed in 2024. Trans activists interviewed by the Washington Blade on 10 April 2025 described the community's situation as chaotic and desperate, with violence, discrimination and poverty reported as worsened. Activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, an increase of 62% year on year and the highest count in the observatory's ten years of operation, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5% of victims (142 cases) and gay men for 22% (50). Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026 and tied the surge to institutional weakening and state legitimation of discriminatory discourse; Catamarca sits under that national pattern with no separate local record.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in the case as it now stands.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina's permissive statutory framework coexists with executive and institutional turbulence that a visitor will encounter before any provincial rule is reached. The closure of INADI removes the federal body that handled discrimination complaints, and the elimination of the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry removed the ministry to which such complaints were routed.

The national direction of travel is measured rather than assumed: the National LGBT+ Hate Crimes Observatory's 2025 count of at least 227 offences rose 62% over 2024 and is the highest in its ten years of operation, which places any single-year comparison from earlier in the decade in a different light.

Argentina's record as the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and the United Nations's description of Law 26.743 as pioneering sit against the Outright International overview of 12 March 2026, which returns negative assessments on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration. The two framings describe different layers of the same regime rather than contradicting each other.

No provincial or municipal data was located for Catamarca, so the national figures carry the assessment; reporting on trans violence in the sources at hand is concentrated in Buenos Aires.
localsOnly:
Residents of Catamarca obtain legal gender recognition through the national process under Law 26.743, which requires no surgery, no hormone treatment and no judicial approval, and through the provincial civil registry that implements it. Nothing in the located sources indicates a separate Catamarca procedure.

The February 2025 decrees bear directly on residents rather than visitors: the ban on gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors restricts care available to adolescents in the province, and the decree on the housing of transgender people in prison governs where a trans resident held in provincial custody would be placed.

The dismissal of trans people hired under the public-sector labour-inclusion quota in 2024 affected residents employed in the provincial and national administration alike, and the closure of INADI removed the channel through which residents would file a federal discrimination complaint.

Provincial anti-discrimination protections exist alongside the national statutes, but no Catamarca-specific enforcement record, complaint tally or court decision was located.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation filed against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is not recorded in the sources available here and remains unresolved.

No Catamarca-specific reporting was located on hate crimes, on enforcement of the gender identity law, on prison housing cases, or on the provincial civil registry's processing of gender-marker changes. The national figures therefore stand in for the province without local confirmation.

Whether the closure of INADI and the elimination of the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry were completed through formal legal instruments or are recorded only through their operational effects is not established in the sources at hand.

The province-level distribution of the 227 hate crimes recorded for 2025 is not broken down in the available material, so no share can be attributed to Catamarca. Whether provincial authorities in Catamarca adopted any response to the 2025 violence record is likewise not sourced.
